claim: AMPA-type receptors (AMPARs) are rapidly inserted into synapses undergoing plasticity to increase synaptic transmission.
source: AMPA-type receptors (AMPARs) are rapidly inserted into synapses undergoing plasticity to increase synaptic transmission, but it is not fully understood if and how AMPAR-containing vesicles are selectively trafficked to these synapses.
evidence: This is a well-established finding in the field of synaptic plasticity, supported by extensive prior research.

claim: GluA1-containing vesicles are confined and concentrated near sites of stimulation-induced structural plasticity.
source: We find that GluA1-containing vesicles are confined and concentrated near sites of stimulation-induced structural plasticity.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental observations using single-particle tracking.

claim: Confinement of GluA1-containing vesicles is mediated by actin polymerization.
source: We show that confinement is mediated by actin polymerization, which hinders the active transport of GluA1-containing vesicles along the length of the dendritic shaft by modulating the rheological properties of the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experiments using actin polymerization inhibitors and rheological probes.

claim: Actin polymerization hinders the active transport of GluA1-containing vesicles along the length of the dendritic shaft by modulating the rheological properties of the cytoplasm.
source: We show that confinement is mediated by actin polymerization, which hinders the active transport of GluA1-containing vesicles along the length of the dendritic shaft by modulating the rheological properties of the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is supported by experiments showing that actin polymerization changes cytoplasmic properties and reduces vesicle motion.

claim: Actin polymerization facilitates myosin-mediated transport of GluA1-containing vesicles to exocytic sites.
source: Actin polymerization also facilitates myosin-mediated transport of GluA1-containing vesicles to exocytic sites.
evidence: This is supported by experiments showing that myosin inhibition reduces lateral transport of vesicles to exocytic sites.

claim: Neurons utilize F-actin to increase vesicular GluA1 reservoirs and promote exocytosis proximal to the sites of synaptic activity.
source: We conclude that neurons utilize F-actin to increase vesicular GluA1 reservoirs and promote exocytosis proximal to the sites of synaptic activity.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, integrating multiple experimental findings.

claim: Synaptic plasticity is regarded as the cellular basis for learning and memory.
source: Synaptic plasticity – the modulation of synaptic connections in response to changes in neuronal activity – is regarded as the cellular basis for learning and memory (Abbott and Nelson, 2000; Citri and Malenka, 2008; Magee and Grienberger, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature in the field.

claim: Changes in postsynaptic spine morphology and protein composition are observed during synaptic plasticity.
source: Changes in postsynaptic spine morphology (i.e. structural plasticity) and protein composition are observed during synaptic plasticity and are thought to contribute to changes in synaptic transmission (i.e. functional plasticity; Kasai et al., 2010; Nakahata and Yasuda, 2018; Kasai, 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Persistent pre-synaptic neurotransmitter release stimulates postsynaptic spine enlargement and insertion of proteins into the synapse.
source: Persistent pre-synaptic neurotransmitter release stimulates postsynaptic spine enlargement and insertion of proteins into the synapse (Matsuzaki et al., 2004; Okamoto et al., 2004; Hayashi and Majewska, 2005; Patterson and Yasuda, 2011), including α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid receptors (AMPARs; Song and Huganir, 2002)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: AMPARs are ionotropic glutamate receptors that permit the influx of sodium, potassium, and in certain cases calcium ions.
source: including α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid receptors (AMPARs; Song and Huganir, 2002) – ionotropic glutamate receptors that permit the influx of sodium, potassium, and in certain cases calcium ions (Chater and Goda, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge about AMPAR function, supported by a citation.

claim: Increase in AMPAR abundance and changes to AMPAR conductance result in a greater inward flow of ions in response to stimulation.
source: This increase in AMPAR abundance, as well as changes to AMPAR conductance, results in a greater inward flow of ions in response to stimulation (Anggono and Huganir, 2012; Diering and Huganir, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The majority of AMPARs are synthesized in the cell body and then enter the secretory pathway.
source: The majority of AMPARs are synthesized in the cell body and then enter the secretory pathway, where they are trafficked in vesicles and inserted into the neuronal membrane via exocytosis (Shepherd and Huganir, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: AMPARs on the membrane can diffuse into synapses.
source: AMPARs on the membrane can diffuse into synapses (Choquet and Opazo, 2022)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: AMPARs can be endocytosed and delivered to lysosomes for degradation or recycled through the endocytic pathway.
source: and can also be endocytosed and delivered to lysosomes for degradation or recycled through the endocytic pathway (Ehlers, 2000; Carroll et al., 2001; Goo et al., 2017; Hanley, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Input specificity is an important feature of synaptic plasticity, where plasticity stimulated at one synapse does not spread to inactive synapses.
source: An important feature of synaptic plasticity is input specificity – plasticity stimulated at one synapse does not spread to inactive synapses (Kandel et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Input specificity suggests that AMPARs are inserted selectively into stimulated synapses.
source: An important feature of synaptic plasticity is input specificity – plasticity stimulated at one synapse does not spread to inactive synapses (Kandel et al., 2013) – suggesting that AMPARs are inserted selectively into stimulated synapses.
evidence: This is an inference based on the property of input specificity.

claim: AMPARs in vesicles are trafficked through dendrites by both microtubule- and actin-based motors.
source: AMPARs in vesicles are trafficked through dendrites by both microtubule- and actin-based motors, and disrupting active transport of AMPARs interferes with long-term potentiation (LTP), a commonly studied form of plasticity (Setou et al., 2002; Hoogenraad et al., 2005; Correia et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2008; Hoerndli et al., 2013; Hoerndli et al., 2015; Wagner et al., 2019; Gutiérrez et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Disrupting active transport of AMPARs interferes with long-term potentiation (LTP).
source: AMPARs in vesicles are trafficked through dendrites by both microtubule- and actin-based motors, and disrupting active transport of AMPARs interferes with long-term potentiation (LTP), a commonly studied form of plasticity (Setou et al., 2002; Hoogenraad et al., 2005; Correia et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2008; Hoerndli et al., 2013; Hoerndli et al., 2015; Wagner et al., 2019; Gutiérrez et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Hangen et al., 2018 found AMPAR vesicles slow down and pause in response to elevated intracellular calcium levels during neuronal activity.
source: Using this technique, Hangen et al., 2018 found AMPAR vesicles slow down and pause in response to elevated intracellular calcium levels during neuronal activity, and consequently hypothesized that a calcium-mediated mechanism primes AMPAR vesicles for exocytosis.
evidence: This is a description of findings from a cited study.

claim: Endosomes containing exogenous AMPARs can enter dendritic spines.
source: Additional studies have demonstrated that endosomes containing exogenous AMPARs can enter dendritic spines (EstevesdaSilva et al., 2015; Bowen et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Scanning electron micrographs of immunogold-labeled AMPARs fail to reveal a substantial fraction of AMPAR vesicles in spines.
source: However, scanning electron micrographs of immunogold-labeled AMPARs fail to reveal a substantial fraction of AMPAR vesicles in spines (Tao-Cheng et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Imaging exogenous AMPARs tagged with super ecliptic pHluorin shows that exocytosis occurs largely at extrasynaptic sites.
source: Moreover, imaging exogenous AMPARs tagged with super ecliptic pHluorin shows that exocytosis occurs largely at extrasynaptic sites (Lin et al., 2009; Makino and Malinow, 2009; Patterson et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: After exocytosis, AMPARs diffuse freely in random directions, but diffusion decreases precipitously at synapses.
source: After exocytosis, AMPARs diffuse freely in random directions, but diffusion decreases precipitously at synapses (Tardin et al., 2003)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: AMPARs are anchored at synapses by postsynaptic density (PSD) proteins, such as PSD-95.
source: because AMPARs are anchored there by postsynaptic density (PSD) proteins, such as PSD-95 (El-Husseini et al., 2000; Bats et al., 2007; Opazo et al., 2010; Opazo et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Synaptic activity changes both the composition of proteins in the synapse and posttranslational modifications on AMPARs, further enhancing receptor anchoring.
source: Synaptic activity changes both the composition of proteins in the synapse and posttranslational modifications on AMPARs, further enhancing receptor anchoring (Opazo et al., 2010; Diering and Huganir, 2018; Lu and Roche, 2012; Opazo et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Crosslinking AMPARs on the neuronal membrane to prevent their diffusion impairs synaptic potentiation in vivo.
source: Importantly, crosslinking AMPARs on the neuronal membrane to prevent their diffusion impairs synaptic potentiation in vivo (Penn et al., 2017; Getz et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The net distance a receptor can travel via diffusion is limited.
source: Nevertheless, the net distance a receptor can travel via diffusion is limited (Groc and Choquet, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: GluA1-HaloTag is trafficked to postsynaptic densities.
source: Using immunofluorescence labeling and STED, we demonstrate that HaloTag insertion at R280 does not disrupt GluA1 trafficking to postsynaptic densities (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B–D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence and STED microscopy data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: GluA1-HaloTag responds to stimulation.
source: GluA1-HaloTag is trafficked to postsynaptic densities and responds to stimulation
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments showing increased surface expression after cLTP.

claim: Insertion of HaloTag at R280 in the NTD of GluA1 does not significantly alter its channel function.
source: Finally, using electrophysiological methods, we demonstrate that insertion of HaloTag at R280 in the NTD of GluA1 does not significantly alter its channel function (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiology data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: cLTP induction results in a significant decrease in the fraction of GluA1-HT vesicles undergoing active transport.
source: When HMM-Bayes is applied to characterize trajectories collected during cLTP induction, we find a significant decrease in the fraction of GluA1-HT vesicles undergoing active transport (Figure 1E, pie charts).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by single-particle tracking data and HMM-Bayes analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The diffusion coefficients for GluA1-HT vesicles undergoing diffusion are significantly reduced by cLTP induction.
source: The diffusion coefficients (D) for GluA1-HT vesicles undergoing diffusion are also significantly reduced by cLTP induction (Figure 1E, histogram).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by single-particle tracking data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Vesicles exhibit increased subdiffusion in response to cLTP induction.
source: In addition, vesicles exhibit increased subdiffusion (i.e. constrained diffusion due to molecular crowding or interactions; Feder et al., 1996; Saxton, 2007) in response to cLTP induction (Figure 1—figure supplement 10).
evidence: This is supported by mean square displacement analysis shown in supplementary figures.

claim: During cLTP, GluA1-HT vesicles have a greater probability of switching from active transport to diffusion than from diffusion to active transport.
source: By contrast, during cLTP, GluA1-HT vesicles have a greater probability of switching from active transport to diffusion than from diffusion to active transport (Figure 1—figure supplement 11C, cLTP, kAT-D vs kD-AT).
evidence: This is supported by HMM-Bayes analysis of state-switching probabilities shown in supplementary figures.

claim: GluA1-HT vesicles undergoing diffusion have a high probability to continue diffusing during cLTP.
source: Furthermore, GluA1-HT vesicles undergoing diffusion have a high probability to continue diffusing (Figure 1—figure supplement 11C, cLTP, kD-D).
evidence: This is supported by HMM-Bayes analysis shown in supplementary figures.

claim: sLTP results in reduced active transport and lower rates of diffusion for GluA1-HT vesicles in Zone 1 but not Zone 2 or Zone 3.
source: We find that sLTP results in reduced active transport and lower rates of diffusion for GluA1-HT vesicles in Zone 1 but not Zone 2 or Zone 3 (Figure 2C–D)
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by single-particle tracking data shown in Figure 2.

claim: sLTP stimulation in the absence of MNI failed to alter the fraction of vesicles exhibiting active transport or the diffusion coefficient of vesicles both proximal and distal to the site of stimulation.
source: By contrast, sLTP stimulation in the absence of MNI failed to alter the fraction of vesicles exhibiting active transport or the diffusion coefficient of vesicles both proximal and distal to the site of stimulation (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B–C)
evidence: This is a control experiment shown in supplementary figures demonstrating specificity of the effect.

claim: GluA1-HT vesicles in Zone 1 imaged 10 min after the cessation of sLTP stimulation exhibited similar motion behaviors to those imaged immediately after the cessation of sLTP.
source: Furthermore, GluA1-HT vesicles in Zone 1 imaged 10 min after the cessation of sLTP stimulation exhibited similar motion behaviors to those imaged immediately after the cessation of sLTP (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A, Active transport bar graph and Diffusion histogram)
evidence: This is supported by time-course data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: sLTP increases the probability that multi-state GluA1-HT vesicles undergoing active transport in Zone 1 switch to and stay in a diffusive state.
source: sLTP increases the probability that multi-state GluA1-HT vesicles undergoing active transport in Zone 1 switch to and stay in a diffusive state (Figure 2—figure supplement 4, sLTP Zone 1, kD-AT vs kAT-D, and kD-D)
evidence: This is supported by HMM-Bayes analysis shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Multi-state vesicles in Zone 2 and Zone 3 have similar probabilities of switching between active transport and diffusion after sLTP.
source: By contrast, multi-state vesicles in Zone 2 and Zone 3 have similar probabilities of switching between active transport and diffusion after sLTP (Figure 2—figure supplement 4, sLTP Zone 2+3, kD-AT vs kAT-D).
evidence: This is supported by HMM-Bayes analysis shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Stimulating neuronal activity leads to elevated intracellular calcium levels and the activation of calcium signaling pathways that trigger the polymerization of actin.
source: We hypothesized that F-actin in the dendritic shaft might be involved because stimulating neuronal activity leads to elevated intracellular calcium levels and the activation of calcium signaling pathways that trigger the polymerization of actin (Okamoto et al., 2004; Okamoto et al., 2007; Okamoto et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Recent studies have reported the rearrangement of F-actin networks in the dendritic shaft during neuronal activity.
source: Moreover, recent studies have reported the rearrangement of F-actin networks in the dendritic shaft during neuronal activity (Schätzle et al., 2018; Lavoie-Cardinal et al., 2020)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: F-actin networks can reposition lysosomes in neurites.
source: and found that F-actin networks can reposition lysosomes in neurites (Katrukha et al., 2017; van Bommel et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: F-actin networks formed in response to sLTP are persistent.
source: Importantly, F-actin networks formed in response to sLTP are persistent (Okamoto et al., 2004)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: During cLTP induction, tractin in the dendritic shaft redistributes into a network of filaments.
source: During cLTP induction, tractin in the dendritic shaft redistributes into a network of filaments (Figure 3A, cLTP).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Airyscan microscopy images shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The combined length of tractin filaments in the dendritic shaft is significantly greater during cLTP.
source: The combined length of these tractin filaments in the dendritic shaft is significantly greater during cLTP (Figure 3A, Tractin length, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by image analysis shown in Figure 3A and supplementary figures.

claim: Treating neurons with LatA prevents redistribution of tractin during cLTP.
source: Treating neurons with LatA not only prevents redistribution of tractin during cLTP, but also reduces the intensity of tractin signal in dendritic spines (Figure 3B, cLTP +LatA)
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with the actin polymerization inhibitor LatA shown in Figure 3B.

claim: cLTP resulted in greater phalloidin labeling in dendritic shafts.
source: cLTP resulted in greater phalloidin labeling in dendritic shafts, while LatA treatment during cLTP decreased phalloidin labeling (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C)
evidence: This is demonstrated by STED microscopy of phalloidin-labeled F-actin shown in supplementary figures.

claim: sLTP significantly reduces the fraction of GluA1-HT vesicles undergoing active transport inside but not outside regions of the dendritic shaft with actin polymerization.
source: By tracking GluA1-HT vesicles after sLTP (Figure 3D and Figure 3—video 1), we find that sLTP significantly reduces the fraction of GluA1-HT vesicles undergoing active transport, as well as the diffusion coefficient of GluA1-HT vesicles, inside but not outside regions of the dendritic shaft with actin polymerization (Figure 3E–F).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by single-particle tracking data shown in Figure 3.

claim: sLTP significantly reduces the diffusion coefficient of GluA1-HT vesicles inside but not outside regions of the dendritic shaft with actin polymerization.
source: By tracking GluA1-HT vesicles after sLTP (Figure 3D and Figure 3—video 1), we find that sLTP significantly reduces the fraction of GluA1-HT vesicles undergoing active transport, as well as the diffusion coefficient of GluA1-HT vesicles, inside but not outside regions of the dendritic shaft with actin polymerization (Figure 3E–F).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by single-particle tracking data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The effect of sLTP on GluA1-HT vesicle motion is disrupted by LatA treatment.
source: Importantly, the effect of sLTP on GluA1-HT vesicle motion is disrupted by LatA treatment (Figure 3G–H and Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with LatA shown in Figure 3.

claim: LatA prevented cLTP-mediated changes in GluA1-HT vesicle mobility.
source: Similarly, LatA prevented cLTP-mediated changes in GluA1-HT vesicle mobility, demonstrating that cLTP-induced actin polymerization results in the confinement of GluA1-HT vesicles as well (Figure 3—figure supplement 5 and Figure 1—figure supplement 11).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with LatA shown in supplementary figures.

claim: There is a significant increase in the number of GluA1-HT vesicles inside, but not outside, regions of actin polymerization after sLTP.
source: After adjusting the number of vesicles for photobleaching (Materials and methods), we find a significant increase in the number of GluA1-HT vesicles inside, but not outside, regions of actin polymerization after sLTP (Figure 3I and Figure 3—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by vesicle counting data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: The increase in GluA1-HT vesicles is blocked by the addition of LatA.
source: Moreover, the increase in GluA1-HT vesicles is blocked by the addition of LatA (Figure 3J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with LatA shown in Figure 3J.

claim: AMPARs interact with myosins Va, Vb, and VI.
source: AMPARs interact with myosins Va, Vb, and VI (Correia et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2008; Nash et al., 2010; EstevesdaSilva et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Myosins Va, Vb, and VI are involved in the calcium-dependent, short-range recruitment of AMPARs in endosomes to and from dendritic spines.
source: which are involved in the calcium-dependent, short-range recruitment of AMPARs in endosomes to and from dendritic spines.
evidence: This is based on prior research on myosin function in AMPAR trafficking.

claim: Inhibition of myosin did not alter the fractions of GluA1-HT vesicles exhibiting active transport, or the diffusion coefficients of GluA1-HT vesicles, either under unstimulated conditions or during cLTP.
source: Inhibition of myosin did not alter the fractions of GluA1-HT vesicles exhibiting active transport, or the diffusion coefficients of GluA1-HT vesicles, either under unstimulated conditions or during cLTP (Figure 3—figure supplement 6B–C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with myosin inhibitors shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Acute pharmacological inhibition of myosin did not affect the fraction of GluA1-HT vesicles exhibiting active transport, or the diffusion coefficient of GluA1-HT vesicles, after sLTP stimulation.
source: Likewise, acute pharmacological inhibition of myosin did not affect the fraction of GluA1-HT vesicles exhibiting active transport, or the diffusion coefficient of GluA1-HT vesicles, after sLTP stimulation (Figure 3—figure supplement 6D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with myosin inhibitors shown in supplementary figures.

claim: F-actin disrupts GluA1-HT vesicle motion in a manner independent of myosin activity.
source: Based on these observations, we conclude that F-actin disrupts GluA1-HT vesicle motion in a manner independent of myosin activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the myosin inhibition experiments.

claim: Treatment of neurons with Jasplakinolide is sufficient to inhibit active transport and reduce the rate of diffusion of GluA1-HT vesicles.
source: Treatment of neurons with Jasplakinolide (Jsp), an F-actin stabilizer that promotes actin polymerization, is sufficient to inhibit active transport and reduce the rate of diffusion of GluA1-HT vesicles (Figure 4A and Figure 4B, left histogram).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with Jasplakinolide shown in Figure 4.

claim: The Jsp-mediated reduction in GluA1-HT vesicle motion is not altered by pharmacological inhibition of myosin.
source: Furthermore, the Jsp-mediated reduction in GluA1-HT vesicle motion is not altered by pharmacological inhibition of myosin, indicating that F-actin itself plays a role in the reduced motion of GluA1-HT vesicles (Figure 4A and Figure 4B, right histogram).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments combining Jasplakinolide and myosin inhibitors shown in Figure 4.

claim: GEM-HT-ST diffusion is significantly reduced during cLTP induction.
source: We find that GEM-HT-ST diffusion is significantly reduced during cLTP induction (Figure 4D, cLTP)
evidence: This is demonstrated by tracking of the rheological probe GEM-HT-ST shown in Figure 4D.

claim: LatA prevents the decrease in GEM-HT-ST diffusion coefficient during cLTP.
source: and this reduction is dependent on actin polymerization as LatA prevents the decrease in diffusion coefficient (Figure 4D, cLTP +LatA).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with LatA shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Actin polymerization stimulated by Jsp is sufficient to reduce the motion of GEM-HT-ST.
source: Moreover, actin polymerization stimulated by Jsp is sufficient to reduce the motion of GEM-HT-ST (Figure 4D, Jsp).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with Jasplakinolide shown in Figure 4D.

claim: sLTP results in a reduction in the rate of GEM-HT-ST diffusion in regions of dendritic shafts where actin polymerization occurs.
source: sLTP also results in a reduction in the rate of GEM-HT-ST diffusion in regions of dendritic shafts where actin polymerization occurs (Figure 4E, sLTP IN vs sLTP OUT)
evidence: This is demonstrated by tracking of GEM-HT-ST after sLTP shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The reduction in GEM-HT-ST diffusion after sLTP is dependent on the presence of MNI.
source: in a manner that is dependent on the presence of MNI (Figure 4E, No MNI IN)
evidence: This is demonstrated by control experiments without MNI shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The reduction in GEM-HT-ST diffusion after sLTP is dependent on actin polymerization.
source: and actin polymerization (Figure 4E, sLTP +LatA IN).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with LatA shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Synaptic activity changes the rheological properties of the dendritic shaft by stimulating actin polymerization.
source: These experiments demonstrate that synaptic activity changes the rheological properties of the dendritic shaft by stimulating actin polymerization.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the GEM-HT-ST diffusion experiments.

claim: Actin polymerization confines GluA1-HT vesicles by altering the properties of the dendritic cytoplasm independent of direct interactions between GluA1 and myosin.
source: Combined with our findings that triggering actin polymerization is sufficient to disrupt GluA1-HT vesicle motion (via Jsp treatment) and that myosin inhibition did not alter activity-mediated changes in motion, these observations are consistent with the hypothesis that actin polymerization confines GluA1-HT vesicles by altering the properties of the dendritic cytoplasm independent of direct interactions between GluA1 and myosin.
evidence: This is a conclusion integrating multiple experimental findings.

claim: GluA1-HT-SEP exocytic events occur at a low rate prior to stimulation, but increase dramatically during cLTP induction.
source: GluA1-HT-SEP exocytic events occur at a low rate prior to stimulation, but increase dramatically during cLTP induction (Figure 5B, cLTP, and Figure 5—video 2), consistent with previous findings (Kopec et al., 2006).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging of GluA1-HT-SEP exocytosis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The increase in GluA1-HT-SEP exocytosis is dependent on actin polymerization.
source: The increase in GluA1-HT-SEP exocytosis is dependent on actin polymerization, as LatA reduces the rate of exocytosis during cLTP induction (Figure 5B, cLTP +LatA).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with LatA shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Acute pharmacological inhibition of myosin disrupts cLTP-stimulated GluA1-HT-SEP exocytosis.
source: Acute pharmacological inhibition of myosin also disrupts cLTP-stimulated GluA1-HT-SEP exocytosis (Figure 5B, cLTP +MI)
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with myosin inhibitors shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Myosin plays a role in regulating exocytosis of GluA1-HT-SEP.
source: suggesting that while myosin does not play a role in disrupting transport of GluA1-HT vesicles, it plays a role in regulating exocytosis of GluA1-HT-SEP.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of myosin inhibition on vesicle transport versus exocytosis.

claim: sLTP stimulation increases GluA1-HT-SEP exocytosis events to a much greater extent proximal than distal to the site of uncaging.
source: sLTP stimulation increases GluA1-HT-SEP exocytosis events to a much greater extent proximal than distal to the site of uncaging (Figure 5C, sLTP).
evidence: This is demonstrated by spatial analysis of exocytosis events shown in Figure 5C.

claim: LatA treatment partially blocks sLTP-mediated increases in GluA1-HT-SEP exocytosis.
source: Similar to their effect on cLTP-mediated GluA1-HT-SEP exocytosis, LatA treatment and acute myosin inhibition both partially block sLTP-mediated increases in GluA1-HT-SEP exocytosis (Figure 5C, sLTP +LatA and sLTP +MI).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with LatA shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Acute myosin inhibition partially blocks sLTP-mediated increases in GluA1-HT-SEP exocytosis.
source: Similar to their effect on cLTP-mediated GluA1-HT-SEP exocytosis, LatA treatment and acute myosin inhibition both partially block sLTP-mediated increases in GluA1-HT-SEP exocytosis (Figure 5C, sLTP +LatA and sLTP +MI).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with myosin inhibitors shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The accumulation of GluA1-HT vesicles near sites of sLTP is spatially correlated with increased exocytosis of GluA1-HT-SEP.
source: We conclude that the accumulation of GluA1-HT vesicles near sites of sLTP is spatially correlated with increased exocytosis of GluA1-HT-SEP, and that local disruption of GluA1-HT vesicle motion and the increase in GluA1-HT-SEP exocytosis are both dependent on actin polymerization in the dendritic shaft.
evidence: This is a conclusion integrating vesicle tracking and exocytosis data.

claim: Local disruption of GluA1-HT vesicle motion and the increase in GluA1-HT-SEP exocytosis are both dependent on actin polymerization in the dendritic shaft.
source: We conclude that the accumulation of GluA1-HT vesicles near sites of sLTP is spatially correlated with increased exocytosis of GluA1-HT-SEP, and that local disruption of GluA1-HT vesicle motion and the increase in GluA1-HT-SEP exocytosis are both dependent on actin polymerization in the dendritic shaft.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experiments with LatA.

claim: The trajectories of GluA1-HT-SEP vesicles that undergo exocytosis have smaller radii of confinement when compared to vesicles that do not exocytose.
source: The trajectories of GluA1-HT-SEP vesicles that undergo exocytosis (Pre-exocytosis) have smaller radii of confinement when compared to vesicles that do not exocytose (Non-exocytosis), demonstrating that GluA1-HT-SEP vesicles are not imported from distal loci immediately prior to exocytosis.
evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis of vesicle trajectories shown in Figure 6B.

claim: GluA1-HT-SEP vesicles are not imported from distal loci immediately prior to exocytosis.
source: The trajectories of GluA1-HT-SEP vesicles that undergo exocytosis (Pre-exocytosis) have smaller radii of confinement when compared to vesicles that do not exocytose (Non-exocytosis), demonstrating that GluA1-HT-SEP vesicles are not imported from distal loci immediately prior to exocytosis.
evidence: This is inferred from the small radius of confinement of pre-exocytosis vesicles.

claim: sLTP increased the fraction of pre-exocytosis GluA1-HT-SEP vesicles exhibiting active transport.
source: Surprisingly, sLTP increased the fraction of pre-exocytosis GluA1-HT-SEP vesicles exhibiting active transport (Figure 6B, bottom line graph, No MNI vs sLTP, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B, Pre-exocytosis).
evidence: This is demonstrated by HMM-Bayes analysis of pre-exocytosis vesicles shown in Figure 6B.

claim: cLTP increased active transport of pre-exocytosis GluA1-HT-SEP vesicles.
source: Similarly, cLTP also increased active transport of pre-exocytosis GluA1-HT-SEP vesicles (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by HMM-Bayes analysis shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Synaptic activity stimulates the active transport of GluA1-HT-SEP vesicles to exocytic sites, even though the net distances they travel are short.
source: These results show that synaptic activity stimulates the active transport of GluA1-HT-SEP vesicles to exocytic sites, even though the net distances they travel are short.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the analysis of pre-exocytosis vesicle motion.

claim: AMPAR-containing endosomes are primarily trafficked along to the length of dendrites by microtubule-based motors.
source: AMPAR-containing endosomes are primarily trafficked along to the length of dendrites by microtubule-based motors (EstevesdaSilva et al., 2015; Setou et al., 2002; Hoerndli et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: AMPAR-containing endosomes can be recruited by myosin Va and Vb to the sites of exocytosis during LTP induction.
source: but can also be recruited by myosin Va and Vb to the sites of exocytosis during LTP induction (Correia et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Pre-exocytosis GluA1-HT-SEP vesicles do not exhibit strong biases for either longitudinal or lateral motion in the absence of stimulation.
source: By contrast, pre-exocytosis GluA1-HT-SEP vesicles do not exhibit strong biases for either longitudinal or lateral motion in the absence of stimulation (Figure 6D, top histogram, No MNI, and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A, Pre-exocytosis vesicles)
evidence: This is demonstrated by directional bias analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Vesicles travel in random directions to exocytic sites in the absence of synaptic activity.
source: indicating that vesicles travel in random directions to exocytic sites in the absence of synaptic activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of directional bias in unstimulated conditions.

claim: When synaptic activity is induced by sLTP, pre-exocytosis GluA1-HT-SEP vesicles have a strong bias for lateral motion.
source: However, when synaptic activity is induced by sLTP, pre-exocytosis GluA1-HT-SEP vesicles have a strong bias for lateral motion (Figure 6D, top histogram, sLTP).
evidence: This is demonstrated by directional bias analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: cLTP induction leads to increased lateral motion for pre-exocytosis GluA1-HT-SEP vesicles.
source: Likewise, cLTP induction also leads to increased lateral motion for pre-exocytosis GluA1-HT-SEP vesicles (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B, Control vs cLTP).
evidence: This is demonstrated by directional bias analysis shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Vesicles move laterally to exocytic sites in response to synaptic activity.
source: These results show vesicles move laterally to exocytic sites in response to synaptic activity, which we speculate is due to vesicles moving from the center to the periphery of the dendritic shaft.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on directional bias analysis, with speculation about the mechanism.

claim: Most pre-exocytosis GluA1-HT-SEP vesicles that move laterally during stimulation exhibit active transport.
source: We first examined the motion states of pre-exocytosis GluA1-HT-SEP vesicles that move laterally during stimulation and find most exhibit active transport (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis of motion states shown in supplementary figures.

claim: GluA1-HT-SEP vesicles move by motor-based transport to exocytic sites.
source: This result suggests that GluA1-HT-SEP vesicles move by motor-based transport to exocytic sites.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that laterally moving vesicles exhibit active transport.

claim: When actin polymerization is inhibited, the fraction of pre-exocytosis GluA1-HT-SEP vesicles exhibiting active transport is significantly reduced.
source: Moreover, when actin polymerization or myosin activity are inhibited, the fraction of pre-exocytosis GluA1-HT-SEP vesicles exhibiting active transport is significantly reduced (Figure 6B, bottom line graph, sLTP +LatA and sLTP +MI).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with LatA shown in Figure 6B.

claim: When myosin activity is inhibited, the fraction of pre-exocytosis GluA1-HT-SEP vesicles exhibiting active transport is significantly reduced.
source: Moreover, when actin polymerization or myosin activity are inhibited, the fraction of pre-exocytosis GluA1-HT-SEP vesicles exhibiting active transport is significantly reduced (Figure 6B, bottom line graph, sLTP +LatA and sLTP +MI).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with myosin inhibitors shown in Figure 6B.

claim: LatA strongly reduces the lateral motion of pre-exocytosis GluA1-HT-SEP vesicles in response to sLTP.
source: Next, we tested the effect of inhibiting actin polymerization on directional bias and find that LatA strongly reduces the lateral motion of pre-exocytosis GluA1-HT-SEP vesicles in response to sLTP (Figure 6D, middle histogram, sLTP +LatA).
evidence: This is demonstrated by directional bias analysis with LatA shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of myosin blocked lateral motion in response to sLTP.
source: Similarly, pharmacological inhibition of myosin also blocked lateral motion in response to sLTP (Figure 6D, bottom histogram, sLTP +MI).
evidence: This is demonstrated by directional bias analysis with myosin inhibitors shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Inhibition of either actin polymerization or myosin activity prevents increased lateral motion of pre-exocytosis vesicles in response to cLTP.
source: Inhibition of either actin polymerization or myosin activity also prevents increased lateral motion of pre-exocytosis vesicles in response to cLTP (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B, cLTP vs cLTP +LatA and cLTP +MI).
evidence: This is demonstrated by directional bias analysis shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Pre-exocytosis GluA1-HT-SEP vesicles are transported laterally by myosin to the sites of exocytosis in response to synaptic activity.
source: Together, these findings demonstrate that pre-exocytosis GluA1-HT-SEP vesicles are transported laterally by myosin to the sites of exocytosis in response to synaptic activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion integrating multiple experimental findings on directional bias and myosin dependence.

claim: Treating neurons with LatA during stimulation results in a decrease in lateral motion and a strong increase in longitudinal motion of GluA1-HT vesicles.
source: However, when GluA1-HT vesicles are treated with LatA during stimulation, we observe a decrease in lateral motion and a strong increase in longitudinal motion (Figure 6—figure supplement 2E, sLTP +LatA and cLTP +LatA).
evidence: This is demonstrated by directional bias analysis shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Inhibition of myosin during stimulation reduces lateral motion but does not increase longitudinal motion of GluA1-HT vesicles.
source: By contrast, inhibition of myosin during stimulation reduces lateral motion but does not increase longitudinal motion (Figure 6—figure supplement 2F, sLTP +MI and cLTP +MI, and Figure 6—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by directional bias analysis shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Inducing actin polymerization with Jasplakinolide while blocking myosin activity reduces longitudinal motion without increasing lateral motion.
source: Moreover, inducing actin polymerization with Jasplakinolide (Jsp) while blocking myosin activity reduces longitudinal motion without increasing lateral motion (Figure 6—figure supplement 2H, Jsp +MI).
evidence: This is demonstrated by directional bias analysis shown in supplementary figures.

claim: F-actin is necessary and sufficient to confine GluA1 vesicle motion near sites of synaptic activity.
source: These observations support our conclusion that F-actin is necessary and sufficient to confine GluA1 vesicle motion near sites of synaptic activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experiments manipulating actin polymerization and myosin activity.

claim: Myosin promotes the surface expression of GluA1 by mediating its active transport to the sites of exocytosis.
source: Nevertheless, myosin also promotes the surface expression of GluA1 by mediating its active transport to the sites of exocytosis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experiments showing myosin-dependent lateral transport and exocytosis.

claim: Neurons utilize actin polymerization in the dendritic shaft to specify the location to which AMPARs are delivered during synaptic activity.
source: Based on these findings, we propose a new model in which neurons utilize actin polymerization in the dendritic shaft to specify the location to which AMPARs are delivered during synaptic activity.
evidence: This is the main model proposed by the study, integrating all findings.

claim: Actin polymerization occurs in the dendritic shaft proximal to the site of synaptic activity, resulting in molecular crowding in the dendritic cytoplasm at this location.
source: First, actin polymerization occurs in the dendritic shaft proximal to the site of synaptic activity, resulting in molecular crowding in the dendritic cytoplasm at this location (Figure 7A–B).
evidence: This is part of the proposed model, supported by experimental data.

claim: Increased crowding inhibits the longitudinal motion of GluA1 vesicles, concentrating intracellular GluA1 near the site of synaptic activity.
source: The increased crowding inhibits the longitudinal motion of GluA1 vesicles, concentrating intracellular GluA1 near the site of synaptic activity (Figure 7A–B).
evidence: This is part of the proposed model, supported by experimental data.

claim: F-actin acts as a substrate for myosin Va and Vb to recruit GluA1 vesicles to the dendrite membrane.
source: F-actin then acts as a substrate for myosin Va and Vb – activated by the influx of calcium (Correia et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2008) – to recruit GluA1 vesicles to the dendrite membrane (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is part of the proposed model, supported by experimental data and citations.

claim: GluA1 vesicles undergo exocytosis at the dendrite membrane, increasing the amount of surface bound GluA1 that can then diffuse into synapses.
source: Here, GluA1 vesicles undergo exocytosis, increasing the amount of surface bound GluA1 that can then diffuse into synapses (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is part of the proposed model, supported by experimental data.

claim: HITI can potentially introduce indels into target genes and knock out copies of Gria1 in some neurons.
source: HITI can potentially introduce indels into target genes and knock out copies of Gria1 in some neurons (Suzuki et al., 2016), but we find a low frequency of indels around the insertion site of HaloTag (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D)
evidence: This is a potential limitation of the method, but the authors show it is not a major concern in their experiments.

claim: Gria1 expression levels in transfected neurons are similar to those in untransfected neurons.
source: and also that Gria1 expression levels in transfected neurons are similar to those in untransfected neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by mRNA quantification shown in supplementary figures.

claim: HITI-mediated editing of Gria1 does not often lead to unwanted mutations, especially those that knock out copies of Gria1.
source: These observations indicate that HITI-mediated editing of Gria1 does not often lead to unwanted mutations, especially those that knock out copies of Gria1.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on sequencing and expression data.

claim: Hangen et al., 2018 found that GluA1 vesicles undergoing active transport had decreased velocity and paused more frequently during cLTP and photostimulation.
source: Hangen et al., 2018 found that GluA1 vesicles undergoing active transport had decreased velocity and paused (i.e. temporarily lost active transport) more frequently during cLTP and photostimulation.
evidence: This is a description of findings from a cited study.

claim: The authors find vesicles switch their motion state to diffusion and rarely switch back to active transport in response to cLTP and sLTP.
source: By contrast, we find vesicles switch their motion state to diffusion and rarely switch back to active transport (i.e. vesicles stably lose active transport) in response to cLTP and sLTP.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study that differs from prior work.

claim: Vesicles exhibit reduced diffusion coefficients after stimulation.
source: Vesicles also exhibit reduced diffusion coefficients after stimulation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study.

claim: GluA1 vesicles are confined, not paused, near sites of synaptic activity.
source: Based on these differences, we conclude that GluA1 vesicles are confined, not paused, near sites of synaptic activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the authors' findings compared to prior work.

claim: F-actin is found at the base of dendritic spines.
source: F-actin is found at the base of dendritic spines (Schätzle et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: F-actin is found in the dendritic shaft in shaft synapses.
source: and in the dendritic shaft in shaft synapses (van Bommel et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: F-actin is found in periodic submembrane actin rings.
source: and in periodic submembrane actin rings (Lavoie-Cardinal et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: F-actin patches position lysosomes in shaft synapses to support AMPAR turnover.
source: For example, F-actin patches position lysosomes in shaft synapses to support AMPAR turnover (Goo et al., 2017; van Bommel et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: AMPARs are primarily transported along the length of the dendrites on microtubules.
source: Previous studies have found that AMPARs are primarily transported along the length of the dendrites on microtubules (EstevesdaSilva et al., 2015; Setou et al., 2002; Hoerndli et al., 2013; Hoerndli et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Short-ranged transport near the site of synaptic activity is mediated by Myosin Va/b.
source: but we and others find that short-ranged transport near the site of synaptic activity is mediated by Myosin Va/b (Correia et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by the authors' findings and citations to prior research.

claim: GluA1 vesicles are transferred from microtubules to actin for local transport.
source: These observations suggest that GluA1 vesicles are transferred from microtubules to actin for local transport.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that long-range transport is microtubule-based while short-range transport is actin/myosin-based.

claim: F-actin-induced crowding results in the detachment of GluA1 vesicles from microtubules prior to attachment and transport on F-actin.
source: The exact mechanism for this exchange is not known but our findings indicate that F-actin-induced crowding results in the detachment of GluA1 vesicles from microtubules prior to attachment and transport on F-actin.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the authors' findings.

claim: F-actin enhances local transport by acting as a substrate for myosin-based cargos, but also by creating a cytoplasmic environment that strongly disfavors microtubule-based transport.
source: Thus, F-actin enhances local transport by acting as a substrate for myosin-based cargos, but also by creating a cytoplasmic environment that strongly disfavors microtubule-based transport (preventing transport away from the stimulated site).
evidence: This is a conclusion integrating multiple findings about the dual role of F-actin.
